topic.en: What the text is about: why Roman harbour works have stood for two thousand years, what analysis of their concrete showed and whether we can build that way today.
topic.kk: Мәтін не туралы: рим айлақ құрылыстары неге екі мың жыл тұр, олардың бетонын талдау нені көрсетті және бүгін солай салуға бола ма.
topic.ru: О чём текст: почему римские портовые сооружения стоят два тысячелетия, что показал анализ их бетона и можно ли строить так сегодня.

paragraphs.text: Along the coast of the Mediterranean there are harbour walls that have stood in the sea for two thousand years. The piers were poured as wet concrete into wooden forms, left to set under water, and then largely forgotten. Modern harbour works do not last nearly as long. A pier built from ordinary reinforced concrete in the twentieth century is usually given a design life of fifty years, and many of them need expensive repairs long before that. The contrast has puzzled engineers for more than a century: a material made without steel, without modern testing and without electricity has outlived materials designed with all three.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The Roman method is not a secret. A handbook written by a Roman architect in the first century BC records the proportions: volcanic ash, lime and lumps of rock, mixed with sea water rather than fresh. The best ash came from the area around the Bay of Naples, and it was valued enough to be carried by ship to building sites across the empire, from the coast of Spain to the eastern Mediterranean. What the handbook does not contain is any explanation of why the mixture survives. It tells a builder what to do, not what happens inside the material once it is under water.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: In modern concrete, sea water is the enemy. Salt works its way through the pores of the mix, reaches the steel bars inside and rusts them; the rust takes up more space than the metal it replaces, and the concrete cracks from within. In the Roman material there is no steel to attack, and sea water does something else entirely. It slowly dissolves part of the volcanic ash, and the dissolved material forms again as crystals in the gaps and cracks of the concrete, binding the whole mass together. The process is slow and it does not stop: the pier grows stronger with age, decade after decade, for as long as the sea keeps washing through it.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Confirming this took cores of ancient concrete, drilled from piers that are still standing and examined in a laboratory. Under the instruments the samples revealed a rare mineral, aluminous tobermorite, which forms in only a few places in the natural world and which chemists had struggled to make in useful quantities. In the ancient cores it had grown in the spaces around the ash, in plate-like crystals that interlock and hold back the spread of cracks. Dating showed that the crystals had gone on forming for centuries after the concrete was poured. The same analysis explained why the material is so uneven: no two samples are alike, because the reaction depends on what the sea brings to each part of the wall.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: A second discovery came from something that had been dismissed for decades. Roman concrete is full of small white lumps, and these were long read as evidence of careless mixing, proof that the lime had not been stirred in properly. Recent work suggests the opposite. The lumps appear when quicklime is mixed in hot rather than slaked first, and they act as a store of reactive material inside the wall. When a crack opens and lets water in, the water reaches a lump, dissolves it and carries the lime into the crack, where it sets and seals the gap. In laboratory tests, cracked samples made with such lumps stopped leaking within two weeks, while samples made without them were still leaking at the end of the experiment.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: None of this means that harbours should now be built the Roman way. The ancient material is far weaker under load than modern structural concrete, and it takes months rather than days to reach the strength it will hold; a contractor who poured it into the foundations of a tower block would be waiting a long time and would then have to explain the results. The right ash is not available everywhere, and shipping it around the world would undo much of the benefit. The realistic uses are structures where slowness is not a problem and long life is: sea walls, breakwaters, coastal defences, and containment for waste that has to stay where it is put for centuries.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The wider argument is about how success is measured. Cement manufacture is responsible for a large share of the world’s industrial carbon emissions, most of it released in the kiln where limestone is burned. Making that process cleaner is one line of attack; building things that do not have to be replaced is another. A sea wall that stands for two hundred years may in the end save more material than one that is twice as strong and is rebuilt every fifty. The Roman piers are not a recipe to be copied, but they are a useful reminder that durability is a form of efficiency.
paragraphs.label: G
